body.heading: Series: one road for everyone
paragraphs: In a series circuit, components are strung along a single path, so the same current must flow through every one of them in turn. The battery's voltage is shared between the components — two identical bulbs in series each get half the voltage, glow dimly, and split the supply between them.

The single path is also the weakness: break it anywhere and everything stops. Old-fashioned Christmas tree lights were wired in series, which is why one failed bulb could darken the whole string and leave you testing bulbs one by one to find the culprit.

body.heading: Parallel: every branch its own road
paragraphs: In a parallel circuit, each component sits on its own branch connected directly across the supply. Every branch receives the full voltage, so each bulb glows at full brightness regardless of how many others are on. The currents through the branches add up to the total drawn from the supply.

Breaks stay local in parallel wiring: if one branch fails or is switched off, the others carry on untouched. The price is that adding branches draws more total current, which is why circuits have fuses and breakers watching the total.

body.heading: Why your home is parallel
paragraphs: House wiring is parallel for obvious reasons once you see the alternative. In a series house, your lamp would dim whenever the fridge started, everything would run at a fraction of full voltage, and one broken toaster would black out the home. Parallel wiring gives every socket the full mains voltage, independently.

The same logic runs a car's electrics and a torch with two batteries arranged for brightness. Whenever you want devices to behave identically and independently, you wire them in parallel; series is reserved for jobs like splitting voltage deliberately — or strings of LEDs designed as a single unit.

description: Series circuits share one path and one fate; parallel circuits give every branch the full voltage. That difference wires your whole home.
